stem: Why should a health system avoid setting a nurse manager's span of control solely by maximizing the number of direct reports?

options.A: Because an appropriate span depends on unit, staff, organizational, and manager factors; an excessively broad span can create an unmanageable workload and is associated with worse workforce and some patient-safety outcomes.
options.B: Because span of control affects payroll only and has no meaningful relationship to manager workload, staff outcomes, or patient-care outcomes.
options.C: Because the largest possible span always improves supervision by allowing one manager to standardize every clinical and staffing decision.
options.D: Because patient acuity, unit complexity, staff skill and stability, and manager experience should be excluded when managerial workload is designed.

rationale: Recent nursing-management research supports treating span of control as more than a simple headcount. A 2024 Delphi study identified determinants involving unit complexity, resource management, staff number/stability/skill mix, manager experience and autonomy, and organizational factors. A 2026 multisite study found wide variation in nurse-manager span and reported associations between larger span measures and nurse turnover and falls, concluding that manageable workloads may improve workforce and patient outcomes. A is therefore the best answer. B through D ignore the multidimensional nature and documented outcome associations.
educational_objective: Recognize nurse-manager span of control as a multidimensional workload-design decision that should account for unit, staff, manager, and organizational factors rather than direct-report count alone.
source_organization: Peer-reviewed nursing-management research indexed by U.S. National Library of Medicine (PubMed)
source_document_title: Impact of Nurse Manager Span-of-Control on Turnover and Patient Safety in Acute Care; Determinants of First-Line Nurse Managers' Span of Control: A Delphi Study
source_locator: 2026 article Abstract — Objective/Results/Conclusions; 2024 Delphi article Abstract — Results identifying unit, professional, first-line nurse manager, and organization determinant categories
source_claim_supported: Nurse-manager span of control is influenced by multiple unit, staff, manager, and organizational factors; broader span measures have been associated with nurse turnover and fall outcomes, supporting manageable rather than maximized workloads.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Printed p.7, Management of Care — manage care to meet client needs, use organizational resources appropriately, collaborate and supervise within care-delivery systems
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — nurse-manager span of control and workload design

source_original.stem: Why should a health system avoid setting a nurse manager's span of control solely by maximizing the number of direct reports?

options.A: Excessive span can contribute to manager overload and reduce support available to staff and care teams
options.B: Span of control affects payroll only and has no documented relationship to managers or staff outcomes
options.C: The largest possible span always improves supervision because one manager can standardize every decision
options.D: Patient acuity, unit complexity, and staff experience should be ignored when deciding managerial workload

source_original.rationale: Research on nurse-manager span of control shows that it is multidimensional and that excessively expanded spans can contribute to manager overload or burnout and lower staff or patient satisfaction. Staffing, complexity, acuity, and manager factors matter.
source_original.source_detail: 2023 concept analysis, PMID 37159015; consequences of expanded span and multidimensional determinants; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Updated the evidence base with 2024 determinant data and a 2026 outcome study, removed the overbroad burnout/satisfaction causal wording, made the multidimensional workload principle explicit, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Recent peer-reviewed primary/consensus nursing-management studies indexed by NLM; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: Evidence updated through a 2026 acute-care span-of-control outcome study plus 2024 Delphi determinants.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final wording uses association rather than causation and is directly supported by the cited results/conclusions and determinant categories.

distractor_audit.A: Correct; reflects multidimensional determinants and manageable-workload/outcome evidence.
distractor_audit.B: Contradicted by published associations with workforce and patient-safety outcomes.
distractor_audit.C: Unsupported absolute claim and contrary to the evidence supporting manageable spans.
distractor_audit.D: Contradicted by identified determinants such as complexity, staff characteristics, and manager factors.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A incorporates both workload determinants and evidence-based outcome considerations.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address organizational rationale; key does not rely on wording length alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care is appropriate because the construct concerns supervision, resource/workload design, and care-delivery organization.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-solved the item using the 2026 and 2024 studies, specifically challenged the original burnout claim against newer evidence, removed unsupported causal precision, and confirmed A remained uniquely defensible.
